A prosodic domain in Shǐxīng is hence divided into one stressed syllable and the remaining unstressed syllables, the tones of which are deleted. sweep_summary: the list of works with stress in the title for Shixing has a single item, Chirkova & Michaud 2009 'Approaching the prosodic system of Shǐxīng', which is already the catalog's deciding source..), so it was copied into our check folder and re-read: the catalog quote is verbatim from §4.1 (postprint pp.14-15) and the paper confirms the 'tonal' coding (three word tones; a culminative stress anchor that is default-initial but shifts right past toneless prefixes/proclitics). Two further first-hand Chirkova sources held by the project were also read: the 2007 Eastling paper 'The stress and tone continuum in Shixing' (word-tone with accent-like culminativity; confirms) and the 2017 ECLL entry §2.1.4 'Tone and stress' (two lexical tones, EP/LP/RP prominence melodies; refines, and with Chirkova & Chen 2013 JIPA explicitly sets the 2009 stress-anchor analysis aside). No new authoritative statement supersedes the current deciding source. nothing left to acquire.

new_statements.citation: Chirkova, Katia & Alexis Michaud. 2009. Approaching the prosodic system of Shǐxīng. Language and Linguistics 10(3):539-568 (HAL postprint hal-00336149v3)
new_statements.locator: HAL postprint §4.1, pp.14-15 (also abstract, p.1: 'The default location of stress is domain-initial.')
new_statements.reading: Shixing is a word-tone language (three contrastive tones on monosyllables and on phonological words). The 'stress' in the 2009 analysis is an abstract culminative anchor for lexical tone: by default on the first syllable of the phonological word, shifted rightward to the first toned syllable when the word begins with toneless prefixes/proclitics, and final (realized as a boundary H) in all-toneless domains. Its position is fixed by tonal specification and morpheme class, never by syllable count or weight, so the catalog's 'tonal' coding stands. The same author's later descriptions (Chirkova & Chen 2013 JIPA; Chirkova 2017 ECLL §2.1.4) drop this autosegmental stress-anchor analysis for a hybrid system of lexically determined Equal-/Left-/Right-Prominent melodies, which the catalog record already notes.

new_statements.quote: p. 15: "Shǐxīng is a tonal language. It has three contrastive tones, namely (i) high, /H/, (ii) rising, /LH/, and (iii) falling, /HL/. The domain for tone in Shǐxīng is the phonological word." [...] "Contrastive tone in Shǐxīng is distributed over the word as a whole, irrespective of the number of syllables." p. 18: "Alternatively, phrases containing enclitics may be subject to tone and stress interaction, with the following regularities applying. The host word for the enclitics is stressed and surfaces its inherent tone. The following enclitic or enclitics are unstressed. They lose their inherent tones and do not acquire any tone from the initial stressed foot. Given that these syllables invariably surface as low, I analyze them as supplied with a phonological L tone before the phonetics"

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's tonal coding (three word tones, domain = phonological word) and is compatible with the existing Chirkova & Michaud 2009 statement of culminative, default domain-initial 'stress' as the anchor for lexical tone: here too the stressed element is the initial host word (the first toned element) and everything after it is unstressed and L. It adds the detail that the stressed domain can widen to host + first enclitic after a monosyllabic host, and that enclitic phrases can alternatively be tonally integrated as one phonological word. It does not itself state a word-internal stress position for polysyllabic lexical words (no rule of the 'stress falls on syllable X' kind),…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Shixing is described as a word-tone language: three contrastive tones (H, LH, HL) whose domain is the phonological word (1-5 syllables), realized as level-tone sequences over polysyllables, with word tones derived from the tone of the first toned element (root) and toneless affixes/enclitics. The sketch gives no word-level stress rule of its own. Stress appears only (a) in Huáng & Rénzēng's observation (p. 13) that [ɿ] and [ɘ] weaken in unstressed syllables and fuse with the preceding stressed syllable, and (b) in the enclitic-phrase analysis (p. 18): the host word (the initial, toned element of the phrase) is stressed and keeps its inherent tone, while the following enclitics are unstressed, lose their tone and surface as L. In phrases with a monosyllabic host followed by two or more enclitics, the stressed domain may extend to host + first enclitic, with the host's tone expanded over that domain and the remaining enclitics unstressed and low. So prominence sits on the leftmost (host) part of the phrase and is tied to tone realization, not to syllable count or weight.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 18: with a monosyllabic host + two or more enclitics, 'the first two syllables of the phrase (i.e. the host word and the first enclitic) may be stressed', e.g. [Hqua=Hji=Ldʑõ] 'be crying', [Ltsʰu=Htʰi=Lrɛ̃] 'the ghost'. Also enclitic phrases may alternatively be treated as phonological words with the tone of the first toned element expanded over the whole phrase (pp. 17-18). Tone (not stress) irregularities: some HL monosyllables behave as LH in compounds ([HLbõ] 'yak' vs. [Lbo-Hmi] 'female yak'); idiosyncratic tones in some words ([Hrõ-Lmi] 'mare' vs. [LHrõ] 'horse'); pronoun, numeral and numeral-classifier tone patterns 'not yet entirely understood' (pp. 18-19).
new_statements.identity_note: The sketch describes the Upper Reaches (Shàngyóu) variety of Shixing spoken in Shuǐluò Township, Mùlǐ County, Sichuan (p. 10: 'The present overview focuses on the Shǐxīng variety spoken in the Upper Reaches of the Shuǐluò River'), following Huáng & Rénzēng (1991) and Huáng et al. (1992) phonological analyses of the same variety. Author's own fieldwork 2005, 2006, 2008.

sources.citation: Chirkova, Katia. 2025. Evidentiality in Shuhi (Tibeto-Burman). Book chapter, HAL hal-04859987, 41 pp.
sources.quote: 'Shuhi is a tonal language with two contrastive tones on monosyllabic words: the low tone (e.g. /jɛ̀/ 'vegetable oil') and the high tone (/jɛ́/ 'buy'). Content morphemes are specified for lexical tone. Grammatical morphemes ... do not occur in isolation, and their lexical tone cannot be determined. In connected speech, the surface pitch contour of grammatical morphemes depends on the tone of their host lexical word (see in detail Chirkova & Michaud 2009).'

sources.citation: Chirkova, Katia. 2017. Xumi language. Encyclopedia of Chinese Language and Linguistics IV:631-642. Brill. HAL hal-00782007. §2.1.4 'Tone and stress'.
sources.quote: Xùmī has two contrastive tones that occur on monosyllabic words: (i) low rising [...] and (ii) high rising [...]. Content morphemes are lexically specified for tone, whereas affixes are toneless. [...] In lexical words longer than one syllable, three tonal patterns are observed: (i) Equal-Prominence pattern (EP) [...] (ii) Left-Prominent pattern (LP): The high f0 peak is realized before the end of the first syllable [...] (iii) Right-Prominent pattern, RP: The high f0 peak is realized within the last syllable [...] the prosodic pattern of the leftmost root determines in many cases the tonal melody of the whole compound domain
sources.note: Author's later description: two lexical tones on monosyllables; polysyllabic words carry one of three lexically determined prominence melodies (EP/LP/RP), the compound melody predicted by the leftmost root's tone. No fixed stress position; the 2009 default-initial-stress anchor analysis is not maintained (Chirkova & Chen 2013 JIPA, HAL hal-01136684, the text layerstate that their hybrid prominence analysis is 'distinct from an alternative autosegmental analysis of the data (as in, for instance, Chirkova & Michaud 2009)').

sources.citation: Chirkova, Ekaterina. 2007. Zai zhongyin yu shengdiao de lianxuti shang kan Shixingyu [Between stress and tone: tones in Shixing and other Qiangic languages]. Eastling / Dongfang Yuyanxue 2:143-152 (HAL hal-00162105v2).
sources.quote: 史兴语是有声调的语言 ... 其声调负载单位不是音节，而据初步分析认定应该是词（即几个音节一个词一个调）' [Shixing is a tonal language ... its tone-bearing unit is not the syllable but, on preliminary analysis, the word]; the prosodic system is characterised as combining tone and stress (结合声调与重音), on a stress-tone continuum, like other Qiangic languages.

sources.quote: The author's fieldwork in 2005 and 2006 confirms these two observations and uncovers a prosodic system with distinctive pitch (here analyzed as word-tone). [...] 沿着这一思路，史兴语也像蒲西拉坞戎语和草登嘉戎语那样，也可以看做为有音高重音的语言，因其体现有高音累积性（一个词一个高调）、可预测性等重音特征 [Along these lines, Shixing, like Puxi Lavrung and Caodeng rGyalrong, can also be regarded as a pitch-accent language, since it shows accent-like properties such as culminativity of high pitch (one high tone per word) and predictability]. Keywords: Shixing; word tone; stress; pitch accent; tone; Qiangic; areal features
sources.locator: English abstract (the text); Chinese body, section on the tone/stress continuum (the text)
sources.note: Analyses Shixing pitch as word-tone with accent-like properties (one high per word, predictability), placing it on the tone/stress continuum; gives no positional stress rule beyond the 2009 paper. Supports the tonal-or-pitch accent coding.
